## What Last Week's Joint Test Assumed

Last week we tested three restrictions at once and read one number off the
output.

- What did that number assume about the errors?
- We tried several specifications before we reported one. What did the
  searching do to the number?
- Collinearity widened a standard error. Did it move the estimate?

Two minutes with your neighbour. The third question is the shape of today:
a fault that costs you precision and leaves the estimate alone.
:::

## Lecture Plan

- **Heteroskedasticity.** The estimates survive, the standard errors do not, and that is why robust is the default.
- **Serial Correlation.** The same damage, but read it as a symptom of something left out rather than a disease to treat.
- **Misspecification.** The one that is different in kind, because it takes unbiasedness away.

::: {.tablenotes}

# Heteroskedasticity

## What Each Violation Costs: Unbiasedness or Precision

**The goal of this section:** say what a non-constant error variance costs
you, and be exact about what it leaves untouched.

```{=latex}
\tabcaption{Each fault against the promise of week six.}
\begin{dgtable}{l c c c}
\thead{Fault} & \thead{Still unbiased?} & \thead{Still best?}
  & \thead{Usual SE right?} \\ \midrule
Heteroskedasticity   & Yes & No & No \\
Serial correlation   & Yes & No & No \\
Wrong shape          & \hl{No} & \hl{No} & \hl{No} \\
\end{dgtable}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
Three rows, and the third one is not a worse version of the first two. It is
a different column that has gone.
:::

## The Error Fans Out With Schooling

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Residuals from the usual fit, plotted
against years of schooling. The band is narrow on the left and wide on the
right: people with more schooling are spread further from the line.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
Nothing about the line is wrong here. The line is in the right place. What
has changed is how far a person is likely to sit from it, and that depends
on where they are along the axis.
:::

<!-- FIGURE 4-1_hetero-fan: residuals against schooling for one sample of
     120, drawn from C_01_01_population_fn(hetero_gain_dbl = 0.18). Zero
     line in grey. Needs the hetero_gain switch in B_04 and nothing
     else. -->

## The Variance of the Slope Under Heteroskedasticity

**The question this answers:** how far would the slope move across repeated
samples when the error variance is not the same for everybody?

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)
= \frac{\sum_{i} (x_i - \bar x)^2 \, \sigma_i^2}
       {\left[ \sum_{i} (x_i - \bar x)^2 \right]^2}
$$

- $\hat\beta_1$: the slope least squares computes from one sample
- $x_i$: years of schooling for person $i$
- $\bar x$: the sample mean of schooling
- $\sigma_i^2$: the error variance for person $i$

::: {.result}
Set every $\sigma_i^2$ equal to the same $\sigma^2$ and this collapses to the
formula from week 6. That is the only difference, and it is the whole
difference.
:::

## Estimating the Slope Variance With Squared Residuals

**The question this answers:** we cannot see $\sigma_i^2$, so what do we put
in its place?

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta_1)
= \frac{\sum_{i} (x_i - \bar x)^2 \, \hat u_i^2}
       {\left[ \sum_{i} (x_i - \bar x)^2 \right]^2}
$$

- $\hat u_i$: the residual left for person $i$ by the fitted line

::: {.defn title="Notation: the error and the residual"}
$u_i$ is the error, which belongs to the population and which nobody ever
sees. $\hat u_i$ is the residual, which belongs to the fit. The robust
standard error is the second standing in for the first, and the hat is
carrying all of that.
:::

<!-- The one derivation this week, in the appendix and set as homework. In
     the room: state the two formulas, point at the one symbol, move on. -->

## Why Robust Standard Errors Are the Default Choice

The estimator is due to @white1980heteroskedasticity, with the same idea
reached independently by @eicker1967limit and @huber1967behavior a decade
earlier. It has been available in every package you will use for forty
years.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The classical standard error and the
robust one for the same slope, as the error is made to fan out more
steeply. The estimate barely moves; the two standard errors come apart.}
```

::: {.takeaway}
Test first and correct afterwards, and your reported standard error depends
on a test you ran and did not report. Use the robust one from the start and
it does not.
:::

<!-- FIGURE 4-1_robust-vs-classical: classical SE and robust SE for the
     slope, plotted against hetero_gain_dbl running 0 to 0.30, one sample of
     120 at each setting, with the point estimate on a second panel or as a
     flat reference line so students see it does not move. Needs the
     hetero_gain switch. -->

## Arguments For and Against Robust Standard Errors by Default

@angrist2017undergraduate argue that most of what an introductory course
teaches about inference can be replaced by the instruction to use robust
standard errors, and that time spent testing assumptions and applying
generalised least squares fix-ups is time badly spent.

::: {.caveat title="The honest qualification"}
In small samples the robust estimator is itself unreliable, and the usual
version is the least reliable of the family. @long2000using and
@imbens2016robust both recommend the corrected variants — the ones your
software calls HC2 and HC3 — once the sample is small or a few observations
carry unusual leverage. @mackinnon1985some is where those variants come
from.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
So: robust by default, and the corrected variant by default too. That is a
one-word change in your code, not a chapter.
:::

## Vote: Which Estimates Are Still Unbiased?

The error fans out with schooling, exactly as in the figure. We fit the
usual line and report the usual standard error.

- The slope is biased and the standard error is fine.
- The slope is fine and the standard error is too small.
- The slope is fine and the standard error is wrong, and you cannot say in
  advance which way.
- Both are wrong.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: what evidence would
settle it?
:::

# Serial Correlation

## Correlated Errors Have the Same Consequences as Heteroskedasticity

**The goal of this section:** put correlated errors in the same place as
heteroskedasticity, and then argue that the correction is usually the wrong
response.

When errors are correlated with each other — adjacent quarters, workers in
the same firm, people in the same town — the estimates are still centred on
the truth and the usual standard error is still wrong. Row two of the table
is row one again.

::: {.result}
Structurally there is nothing new here. What is new is what you should do
about it, and it is not the same thing.
:::

<!-- IDEA 2. 38-63 min. This module is cross-sectional, so serial
     correlation arrives as an idea rather than as a dataset. That is the
     right weight for it: the transferable lesson is the diagnosis, not the
     HAC formula. -->

## What a Run of Same-Signed Residuals Indicates

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Residuals in order of schooling. They
are negative at both ends and positive through the middle — not scattered,
but arranged in runs.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
Order these residuals by anything and you can compute a correlation. Here
the pattern is not noise that happens to be correlated. It is the shape of
something the model does not contain, showing through.
:::

<!-- FIGURE 4-1_runs: residuals from the straight-line fit, plotted in
     order of schooling, sample of 120 from
     C_01_01_population_fn(curvature_dbl = -0.09). Shade the runs of one
     sign. Needs the curvature switch. The point of drawing it from the
     curvature population rather than a time series is that the two faults
     produce the same picture. -->

## Why Correcting the Standard Error Comes Last

A correction exists: @newey1987simple gives a standard error valid under
both heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation, and it is one argument in your
regression call.

::: {.caveat title="Why reaching for it first is the mistake"}
The correction widens the interval around a number you have not yet asked
whether you should be reporting. @granger1974spurious is the case that
settled this: two unrelated series, a large $t$-statistic and residuals that
were badly correlated. The residuals were the warning. A wider interval
around a meaningless coefficient is still meaningless.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Correlated residuals are a symptom. Ask what is missing, or what shape is
wrong, before you ask which standard error to report.
:::

## Vote: What Would Cause This Pattern?

Residuals negative at both ends of the schooling range and positive through
the middle.

- The errors are genuinely correlated with each other.
- A variable that matters is missing from the model.
- The relationship is curved and we fitted a straight line.
- You cannot tell from this plot which of the three it is.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: what evidence would
settle it?
:::

# Misspecification

## Why the Wrong Functional Form Costs Unbiasedness

**The goal of this section:** show that getting the shape wrong is a
different kind of failure from the first two, and a worse one.

Returns to schooling diminish. The truth bends, and we fitted a line. The
line is then too low in the middle of the range and too high at the ends,
which means the error does not average zero at every level of schooling.

::: {.result}
That is assumption two, the one week 6 said buys unbiasedness. Break it and
the estimate is no longer centred on anything in particular. No standard
error repairs that, because there is nothing wrong with the standard error.
:::

<!-- IDEA 3. 66-92 min. Go back to the table and point at the row. The
     third column is the one that changed. -->

## Curvature and Outliers in the Residual Plot

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Left: residuals against fitted values
with curvature switched on — an arch, not a cloud. Right: the same plot with
a few very high earners in the sample — a cloud with four points a long way
above it.}
```

The point that summary statistics cannot be trusted to reveal a shape is
@anscombe1973graphs, and it is fifty years old and still the reason the
first thing you do with a fitted model is plot it.

::: {.tablenotes}
Two plots, two faults, two different responses. The arch says the model has
the wrong form. The four points say a handful of people are unlike the rest,
and neither a robust standard error nor a quadratic term is the answer to
that.
:::

<!-- FIGURE 4-1_resid-fitted: two panels. Left, residuals against fitted
     values from a sample of 120 drawn with curvature_dbl = -0.09. Right,
     the same plot from a sample drawn with outlier_share_dbl = 0.04 and
     curvature off. Same axes on both so the shapes are comparable. Needs
     the curvature and outlier_share switches. -->

## What the RESET Test Can and Cannot Tell You

There are named tests for this. @ramsey1969tests is the standard one, and it
adds powers of the fitted values to the regression and asks whether they
help.

::: {.caveat}
It will reject for a missing variable, for the wrong functional form, for a
handful of outliers, and for a sample large enough that any of the three is
detectable. A rejection is a prompt to look at the plot. It is not a
diagnosis, and it is certainly not a repair.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Run the plot first. If you run the test first you will spend the afternoon
choosing a correction for a fault you have not identified.
:::

## Ranking the Three Faults by What They Cost

::: {.takeaway title="The claim to take away"}
A wrong standard error costs you an honest interval around the right number.
A wrong shape costs you the number. Almost everyone worries more about the
first, because it is the one with a test attached.
:::

@king2015robust make a related argument that is worth holding on to: when the
robust and the classical standard errors differ a lot, that gap is
information about the model, not just a nuisance to be corrected away.
Something in the specification is not doing its job.

::: {.tablenotes}
This is why the third row of the table is set apart, and why 4.2 exists.
:::

## Vote: Does This Residual Plot Worry You?

A cloud of residuals against fitted values, plus four points sitting far
above the rest — the four highest earners in the sample.

- Yes, and I would use a robust standard error.
- Yes, and I would look at who those four people are.
- Yes, and I would drop them.
- No, four points out of a hundred and twenty is nothing.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: what evidence would
settle it?
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it
means? And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

[Candidate this week: a robust standard error makes the interval honest
about noise. It says nothing about whether the line is the right shape, and
nothing at all about whether schooling is what moved earnings.]

## Application

Take one sample. Fit the usual line. Report the classical and the robust
standard error side by side, then turn the fan on and do it again.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote first: as the error fans out more steeply, does the estimate move, does
the classical standard error move, does the robust one, or some combination?
Take the vote before anything is run.
:::

Lab this week: turn on curvature instead and watch the same two standard
errors both stay narrow while the estimate walks away from the truth.

<!-- 97-105 min. ConcepTest 4. The lab half is the lecture's argument in
     one screen: the diagnostics that get attention respond to the fault
     that matters least. -->

## What Each Fault Costs You

Today was three separate ideas, sorted by what each one takes away:

::: {.contributions}
1. **Heteroskedasticity.** The estimates survive and the standard errors do not, which is why robust is the default rather than a repair.
2. **Serial Correlation.** The same damage with a different cause, and the correction is usually the wrong first move.
3. **Misspecification.** This one takes unbiasedness, and no standard error can give it back.
:::

::: {.caveat title="Where 4.1 stops and 4.2 begins"}
Everything today was a fault you can see in the residuals and respond to.
Next week is the faults no diagnostic will ever reveal, because the residual
plot looks perfectly fine.
:::

## {.plain}

## Derivation: Why Heteroskedasticity Breaks the Variance Formula

Take the week 6 decomposition of the slope into the truth plus a weighted
sum of errors, and compute its variance without assuming the errors share a
variance.

::: {.tablenotes}
Three steps. Write the slope as the truth plus a sum of weights times
errors. Take the variance of that sum, which is the sum of the squared
weights times the individual error variances. Then stop, because there is no
common $\sigma^2$ to pull out. Week 6 pulled it out in one line and never
said that was a step; this is that step, refused. The result is the first
formula on the slide, and the second formula is what you get by putting
$\hat u_i^2$ where $\sigma_i^2$ stands. Why that substitution works is the
interesting part: you cannot estimate $n$ variances from $n$ observations,
but you never needed to — only one weighted sum of them.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

## Notes and Tools

- `plot(model, which = 1)`: residuals against fitted values, which is the
  first thing to look at and the last thing anyone does.
- `sandwich::vcovHC()` with `lmtest::coeftest()`, documented in
  @zeileis2004econometric. Its default is HC3.
- `estimatr::lm_robust()`, which reports HC2 with an adjusted degrees of
  freedom out of the box.
- `fixest::feols()` with `vcov = "hetero"`, if you are already using it.
- Stata's `vce(robust)` is HC1, which is not the same choice; say which one
  you used.
